inquiries.title: A reflection on the past five inquiries, May to November 2024
inquiries.summary: The sixth gathering was a reflection rather than an inquiry. The circle revisited the five inquiries held between May and October 2024, one storyboard at a time, heard from those who had taken each call to action, and then asked one open-ended question each in place of debate. The questions gathered are to be added to the storyboards, so whoever carries an inquiry forward has more to work with.

meeting.landAcknowledgement: No land acknowledgement was given. Indigenous knowledge and governance appeared later, inside the recap of the October inquiry on coexistence with nature, not as an acknowledgement of place.

contextNotes: Not an inquiry: a reflection over the five inquiries held between May and October 2024, revisiting each storyboard rather than opening a new question.

The five revisited storyboards covered preparing families for emergencies, a modern work ethic, helping families afford housing, mentoring adolescents into adulthood, and peaceful coexistence with nature.
Announced as special and exploratory; the hosts explained the sequence for reflection as they worked through it, and asked for suggestions on the format.
Two hosts ran the session, scheduled for about an hour and a half; the forum closed at about an hour and twenty minutes.
Each inquiry followed the same pattern: a storyboard overview, an update from whoever had taken the call to action, then questions only.
Questions only means one open-ended question per person, a five Ws or a how question, with no answer expected; the questions are collected to refine and republish the storyboard.
No hands raised was named as a valid choice, and a question could be typed in the chat instead.
Reflective prompts were offered to whoever carries an inquiry: where the volunteering came from, what has shaped the thinking since, and where to go next.
Held on a Sunday, with participants joining at different points of the weekend.
Participants joined from Canada, Los Angeles, Pittsburgh and Virginia.
Attendance across the earlier gatherings was uneven: one participant had missed all of the prior meetings, and others had attended some and missed others.
One participant joined late after trouble connecting.
Two participants stepped away briefly during the session and returned, each posting a note in the chat.
One participant's microphone carried feedback, and parts of that contribution are unclear in the recording.
The member who had volunteered for two of the calls to action was absent; the hosts undertook to bring the refined storyboards back to that member as encouragement to continue.

Some calls to action had little to report: a planned conversation with a local beekeeper had not happened because of overlapping leave, and accountability to the group was named as the reason for asking anyway.
No survey was run. A survey tool was still in development, with feedback invited through the website or directly to either host.
Administrative notes covered the group's website, theendeavor.net, storyboards published with hyperlinked sources, and social media on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and Quora.

Chat carried material the audio did not: a follow-up placing Virginia's filial responsibility laws in the 1920s, a Los Angeles nonprofit working on housing rights, and reading on AI and the future of work posted near the close and read out by the facilitator.
Chat timestamps run about sixteen and a half minutes ahead of the recording clock; the meeting was open before recording began.

The recording continues for about four minutes after the forum closed, with the hosts discussing how to onboard newer members onto the group's collaboration tools; that stretch is administrative and is not part of the record.
No date was announced for the next Lyceum; the hosts stayed on afterwards for follow-up questions.

reviewed.topic: How do we prepare ourselves and our families to handle emergencies? (the 24 May storyboard)
reviewed.discussion: The facilitator walked the storyboard section by section: the Hawaiian concepts of Ohana and Calabash, godparents and a designated support network, extended relatives near and far, the military family care plan and the bug out bag, and differing views in the United States on whether adult children are expected to care for aging parents. Sources and inputs turned on state law differing from federal law, with Virginia and Texas contrasted, and Medicaid raised. Opportunities were the end of life conversations that get put off, on the reasoning that silence transfers stress and financial burden to surviving family. Challenges were the cost of legal advice and the fact that advance care options vary by state or province. The participant who had taken the call to action was absent; a second participant, who had offered to help compile Virginia information, reported back. The circle then moved to questions only. One asked how responsibility is enforced when a death and the next of kin fall in different states, and how that works across an international border. Another agreed that was the same question, saying the within-country rule was easy enough to grasp but cross-border rules were beyond them. A third said something similar exists in China, asked how the Virginia law came about and who started it, and said they disagree with the law and could give philosophical reasons. The facilitator said it is questionable to hold someone legally or financially responsible for what they may not be able to assume, and undertook to carry the refined storyboard back to the absent volunteer so the volunteer knows the group is still working on it.
reviewed.progress: Contact between the two had been brief only. Research had confirmed that Virginia filial responsibility laws are real: an adult child who is able to earn income can be legally obliged to support a parent in need, and failure to support carries a fine of up to 500 dollars and up to 12 months in jail. The participant reporting had been a disbeliever until checking, and said the volunteer who raised it was right. The origin of the law had not been researched - no forensics on how it came to exist - and looking into that was offered as work for the next gathering, jointly with the absent volunteer. Later in the session, roughly 47 minutes into the recording, chat added that Virginia filial responsibility laws date back to the 1920s. Nothing else had been done on this inquiry since May.

reviewed.topic: What should we strive for in a modern work ethic?
reviewed.discussion: The recap set a military and civilian parallel side by side: an anecdote of engineers on a small team being the standouts while the men around them needed more of a guiding hand, contrasted with a medical field where women students were seen as ready and men less so, leading the circle to ask why women are perceived as having to work twice as hard for the same success. Applications were about hiring: whether interview panels and reference checks ask about soft skills, resilience and continuous learning rather than duties performed. Sources and inputs were intercultural skill and the ability to code switch on globalized teams, with a willingness to learn the other person's background treated as a team-building requirement. There was little regulation to draw on, beyond distinguishing the private and public sectors. Opportunities were investment in human capital - paid time off, retirement contributions, and interviewing staff to inform engagement rather than governing by policies written long ago. The challenge recorded was the end of loyalty to a single employer. In questions only, one participant turned the inquiry toward AI: how it will influence a modern work ethic, what the threats are, what it could replace, and whether soft skills keep people ahead. The facilitator asked whether policies written before the rapid increase of technology need overhauling. Another participant answered from government service that the persistent struggle has not been AI but teleworking - the technology exists, the call itself proves it works across the world, smaller organizations have embraced it and found it effective, and larger ones remain slow. Late in the session an essay by the chief executive of Anthropic and a recorded interview with the same author were posted to chat as further reading on AI and work; the facilitator accepted them and said they would be added to this storyboard.
reviewed.progress: The call to action had two strands. The first was a book recommendation, Athena Rising, on how men can act as role models to open opportunity for women; it surfaced again later in the session among mentorship reading. The second strand, conversations with a small team of engineers on a small team about their understanding of continued government service, was reported on at length. The small team the volunteer supervises had met a work environment described as less than supportive rather than toxic: nobody went out of their way to trip them up, and nobody was actively mentoring them, which wrecked havoc on their professional growth. The remedy applied was ordinary mentorship - paying attention, asking questions other than yes or no, taking genuine interest in professional development - and the report was that the team is now thriving and only needs keeping motivated. The origin of that approach was given as an earlier memory: a slight man struggling with a box on the pier would be helped by everyone, and a woman of the same build would be walked past. The specific question the call to action was set up to answer, how the team views continued government service, went unanswered.

reviewed.topic: How can we help families afford housing in our community?
reviewed.discussion: The recap ran through local farmers under-bidding at auction so an evicted family could stay, the scale of the profit incentive in real estate, and tourist destinations where landlords earn more from short term rentals than from permanent residents building wealth through ownership. Applications were Finland's mandates for low rent and rent control, New York City where one generation benefited from affordable housing and the benefit did not pass to the next, and Hampton Roads, where private companies profit from military post housing of questionable quality. Sources and inputs were systemic racism in housing policy by way of The Color of Law, the Fair Housing Act of 1968 and the gap between its passage and its implementation, and homelessness as a multi-spectrum problem - affordable housing, lack of employment, lack of credit converging - so complex that it paralyzes people out of taking part. Policies considered were rent to own, limiting private development in favor of public, and community land trusts letting nonprofits hold land while tenants buy the housing on it. Opportunities were the Broad Creek housing complex in Norfolk, Virginia as a rent to own route, and extending housing benefits to workers in critical fields so they can plant roots rather than commute from a far suburb. The challenge was that housing is an interagency effort mistaken for one agency's sole responsibility. In questions only, one participant asked what incentives Vancouver offers a private owner of a multifamily building to open a percentage of units to people in this situation. The question drew a long silence before any reply. Afterwards the questioner asked whether it had been heard at all, having spoken at length unsure the mute button was off; the facilitator confirmed it had been heard. The reply named no incentive; the facilitator said the storyboard would keep being updated and that this is not Vancouver's problem alone but the future of large population centers unless public and private sectors act together. A Los Angeles nonprofit that works on housing rights was posted to chat and acknowledged in the room about three minutes later.
reviewed.progress: This call to action was carried by one participant, with a view to partnering with organizations addressing poverty in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside. Real work had happened. In the first year, the priority had been understanding the environment and who is already there, and using the inputs from the August gathering several nonprofits working with unhoused people had been met, all working together and each approaching it from a different angle. The obstacle brought back was circular: someone recovering from substance use needs employment, employment applications need an address, and an unhoused person has no address. The second finding was that organizations exist to hold nonprofit housing providers and government officials accountable, against the complaint that government money for single room occupancy housing goes to paying employees rather than improving the buildings.

reviewed.topic: How do we mentor adolescents into adulthood? (stated in the room as ages 15 and up)
reviewed.discussion: The recap covered the balance in parenting between freedom and absolute freedom, the theory of constant cultivation that moves children through a checklist of activities, and technology as a surrogate educator whose information is sometimes validated and sometimes not. Applications were responsibility thrust on children early by design or by circumstance, living abroad in Germany increasing autonomy, Japan where young children walking to and from school alone is a cultural norm, and a caregiver gap in the United States created by military training and deployment, which creates a condition for poverty. Sources and inputs were negotiation as a life skill and the question of when children get to negotiate for autonomy, and whether surrogate mentors arrive when a caregiver is absent - and whether their absence creates harmful coping mechanisms carried into adulthood. Policies were flexible work and paid time off as a route to parental involvement beyond weekends and holidays. Opportunities and challenges were volunteer mentorship near schools, the varying quality of social media platforms and when to teach a safe presence online, learning what today's youth actually like rather than demanding they learn what an earlier generation learned, and a shortage of mentors in all communities. In questions only the facilitator asked whether any organization carries mentorship across the line into legal adulthood, calling 18 to 28 a vulnerable stretch because decisions now carry legal consequences, and whether organizations pass the torch from 17 into 18 and beyond. One participant said programs for that band would have to be researched. Another made a plug for earlier interdiction: a terrible decision at 16 is permanent in certain jurisdictions, and mentoring a child after a life altering decision, or from behind bars, is a poor substitute for mentoring before it. A third accepted the point as proactive rather than reactive and asked what criteria organizations actually use to designate at-risk youth - whether a young person must already have deviated or been caught, or whether some other factor identifies risk before anything has gone wrong. A fourth proposed that mentoring start before students leave high school, with a professional inside the school to talk to and to encourage a young person to find what interests them, noting that in some communities a counselor is hard to come by. The facilitator cited student support services in Canada as an example, asked what happens when a school has no such staff or one guidance counselor for an entire student body, and recalled military recruiters coming into a high school in a military town, asking what the comparable outside visitors are in towns that get none.
reviewed.progress: Two participants had taken this call to action and one was absent, so the plan to research how communities from local to international scale address mentoring, using social media, went unreported. The other reported a real survey of what already exists, done by reading, general internet search and ordinary community involvement. Mentoring organizations turned out to be plentiful and mostly aimed at at-risk youth and high school ages: the YMCA, state behavioral health services, the Up Center, the Boys and Girls Club of America, and Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts. The Up Center's Team UP was singled out as dating only from 2008 and covering ages 6 to 17. The shape of the commitment was described as a mentor signing up, being matched with a mentee, and giving a couple of hours a week, through government at state, federal or city level, through school systems, or through nonprofits. The route in most often runs through activities already close at hand; this participant had become a volunteer official with USA Swimming and now gives several hours a month to officiating meets. Alongside the organizational route, the report described direct conversation with young people about their use of social media, what they study, what they want after high school - college, a vocational program - and money, noting that a first car is the immediate goal and saving toward a house or any longer-term aim had not occurred to them. Reading on mentorship was offered to the group, and the participant undertook to take the evening's questions back into further research. One planned strand, looking into a school unit, had not been done.

reviewed.topic: How do we cultivate peaceful coexistence with nature in our communities?
reviewed.discussion: The recap was drawn from international examples: the Ganges in India as a holy site flooded with toxic waste from industry and from religious ceremony, and Venus as a planet once like Earth whose atmosphere changed until it was uninhabitable, offered as a possible warning. Applications were India using the court system to extend rights to land, water and air as human rights are understood, and the Chesapeake Bay Foundation in Virginia building a grassroots culture of care for a watershed regardless of a person's industry or private life. Sources and inputs were an uncomfortable truth - a psychological barrier against discomfort leads people to disengage from a complex problem that is happening to them, which limits their citizenship - and the need for those holding the levers of power, corporations and governments, to lead by example. Policies included the contrast between Los Angeles before Covid and during it, when the sky was visible and there was less smog, and environmental racism, where marginalized populations carry greater health hazards through unclean drinking water or land too contaminated to farm. Opportunities were increasing indigenous governance so indigenous knowledge shapes policy, with the David Suzuki Foundation in Canada named as a champion of that, and conservation taught through routine play and exploration inside the school curriculum. Challenges were engaging the older population for cultural wisdom to pass on, and the poor fit between collectivist ideas and communities leaning into purely capitalist thought. An administrative change was reviewed alongside this storyboard: it was the first to carry hyperlinks to the underlying material, the summaries are being hung on the group's website, and the circle was asked for suggestions on the format and for anything that would improve it. The facilitator closed the section by asking whether organizations in government and people in the private sector using their wealth for sustainability are being highlighted in the media in a way that draws others in, or whether those examples are lost to a current atmosphere of fear that prevents shared understanding on climate change. No further questions came.
reviewed.progress: Nothing had happened. The call to action was to speak with a local beekeeper, a work associate of one participant, about how the protection of pollinators is organized and encouraged, and to ask whether the beekeeper would come to a future gathering to speak. The two had not connected: one had been on leave, then the other, and follow-up was deferred until a return to work. The facilitator accepted this and restated the purpose - that the group helps hold each other accountable to what its members say they will do - and repeated the invitation for the beekeeper to join for a short stint.

learned.text: The reflection ran as an untested format. A sequence for reflection stood in place of the Sequence of Inquiry, and the facilitator said so openly rather than presenting it as settled practice.
Reflection exists to hold the circle accountable. Revisiting an inquiry is how a volunteer is reminded of what was undertaken.
Questions only produces refinement rather than answers. Questions harvested from the circle are folded back into the storyboard, which is then republished for whoever carries the call to action.
Silence is a sanctioned response. Raising no hand counts as participation, and the chat box is an equal route into the record.
Volunteers arrive with little or nothing to report, and the format absorbs that rather than penalising it. Of five calls to action revisited, one had barely started and one had stalled entirely.
Life outside the circle is treated as an expected cause of stalled work, not a failure of the volunteer.
Attendance is intermittent, and the reflection serves the people who missed gatherings. Participants who had been absent said the retrospective let them reach inquiries they had not been present for.

changed.text: Reflection becomes an ongoing part of the cycle. Volunteers carrying a call to action are expected to give a short update against set reflective prompts on where they started, what has shifted their thinking, and where to go next.

Storyboards will also be sent to participants by email on request.

storyboard.logline: A reflection rather than an inquiry: five gatherings from May to November 2024 were put back on screen in order, the volunteers who had carried each one said what had come of it, and every pass closed by collecting questions instead of answering them.
storyboard.arcNotes:
This gathering has no inquiry question and must not be given one. It was announced from the first minute as a reflection on past inquiries, and its structure is a loop repeated five times: a storyboard put up and narrated for about three minutes, a report-back from whoever had taken that inquiry's call to action, then a questions-only round in which each participant asks one open-ended question that nobody answers. The questions are recorded, used to refine the storyboard, republished, and left as prompts for the person carrying the work. The evening's shape is therefore an opening, five review passages, a short administrative passage, a fellowship circle, and a close.

The reflection covered 24 May, 30 June, 4 August, 15 September and 20 October 2024. The May gathering, recorded elsewhere as the founding circle, carried an inquiry of its own on preparing families for emergencies. Of the five calls to action, two had moved substantially (the housing volunteer's first year in a new city and its nonprofits, and the mentorship volunteer's survey of organizations), one had moved a short distance (a legal finding on filial responsibility, reported on behalf of an absent volunteer), one had not moved at all (a planned conversation with a local beekeeper, missed because both parties were on leave), and one was held by a participant who was not present. The facilitators named this openly as the accountability function of gathering: life gets in the way, and the circle exists partly to keep each other to what was said.

The questions-only discipline is visible in its failure mode as well as its intent. A question about what incentives a city offers a private multifamily owner to open units drew no answer at all, a long silence, and then a general commitment to keep updating the storyboard; the questioner assumed the mute button had been on, and had in fact been heard. The record keeps the question standing, because the format is built to absorb questions rather than resolve them.

Chat contributions are placed where the circle took them up aloud, not at chat-clock time. The chat clock runs ahead of the recording clock by at least 990 seconds, which the transcript itself confirms: a reading on AI and work posted in chat is acknowledged aloud at @1:14:51. One chat contribution that dates the Virginia filial responsibility laws to the 1920s is deliberately not placed in any beat, because the moment the circle received it cannot be fixed from the recording; it belongs to the emergencies inquiry and should be carried on that storyboard instead.

Source quality: the transcript garbles proper nouns consistently, including the facilitator's own name, the word Lyceum, and Hampton Roads (rendered once as "Panther Roads"). One participant joined on a poor connection and several of that person's sentences are only partly recoverable; the substance recorded in beat 11 is what could be established from the surrounding exchange, not from the broken cues alone.

Suppressions, described without disclosing them. No participant is named anywhere, and roles that would identify one person are dropped, including a family relationship between two people in the circle. The personal name of a non-attendee who may be invited to a future gathering is withheld and the role kept. One participant's family composition is left out, as is a school-affiliated activity belonging to a participant's child, which together would narrow the family to a single school. A contact email address posted in chat for an outside organization is not reproduced, though the organization's purpose is. The identities of two absent volunteers are withheld and recorded as participants not present. From the informal stretch after the close, three things are left out: a private individual named in passing, an on-screen device label and background image, and account-provisioning details attached to named individuals; the substantive onboarding problem is kept.

beats.title: An evening that is not an inquiry
beats.summary: The facilitator opened by naming what made this gathering different. It is a reflection on past inquiries rather than a new one: a reminder for those who took part, and for anyone hearing the inquiries for the first time, an invitation to find what they could contribute. The agenda was walked through: the vision, a moment of collective mindfulness, shared understanding, the sequence for reflection, a pass over the past five inquiries, administrative notes, and a closing fellowship circle. The vision was given as unity and freedom for all, traced to the preamble of the United Nations charter on the dignity and the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family lying in the foundations of freedom, justice and peace, and to the writer bell hooks on culturally diverse education as the practice of freedom. The how was named as the endeavor, a philosophy of shared purpose held across physical distance by technology. The what was named as the Lyceum, a form of cross-cultural learning and problem solving with its name taken from Greece. The co-facilitator added a second reading of the same three terms: technology as ground for a cultural or intelligent revolution rather than a violent one, attention to what makes people alike rather than different, disagreement treated as permissible, and a way forward that is a win-win across cultures, languages, regions and economic boundaries.
beats.pullQuote: coming together and talking about issues and acknowledging that it's okay to it's okay to disagree.
beats.slideHint: Title slide reading Lyceum, a reflection of past inquiries, with the agenda beneath it as six lines. Then a vision slide carrying the United Nations preamble phrase and the bell hooks line. Then a why, how, what triptych: unity and freedom for all; the endeavor, shared purpose across distance; the Lyceum, cross-cultural learning and problem solving.

beats.title: Grounding, two maps, and the norms
beats.summary: The circle was invited to soften the gaze or close the eyes for five guided breaths, each with a gratitude prompt: the earth that sustains and nurtures all life, humanity and the natural world; the ancestors and family who came before; the self, on the ground that looking inward finds peace and love that can then be turned outward to a community; family and friends who support, guide and inspire; and a last breath on the reason for the work, which is not the self but giving children the chance of a better future. Shared understanding followed with the two maps carried over from previous gatherings, one from the United Nations and one from the World Bank colored by region, offered as a memory aid for a group that is not made of geographers, with a suggestion to note the color of where one lives and where one has travelled so that lived experience can be brought to bear. The norms were then restated: respect as the golden rule and the law of reciprocity, about an hour and a half together, deep discourse on the inquiries of the past five or six months, a raised hand to speak, and the chat box for anything outside the conversation.
beats.pullQuote: the reason why we do what we do is not for ourselves.

Then the United Nations country map beside the World Bank regional map with its color key in the top left. Then a norms slide: respect, ninety minutes, raised hand or chat box.

beats.title: The sequence for reflection, and the first storyboard
beats.summary: The mechanics were explained before anything was revisited. Each storyboard would go up and be narrated for about three minutes. Participants were asked to note their questions while listening rather than adding detail to the board. A questions-only round would follow, one open-ended question each, a five Ws or a how. The questions are not answered in the room: they are recorded, used to refine and republish the storyboard, and left as prompts of curiosity for whoever carries that inquiry forward. Raising no hand was named as a choice, and the chat box as an equal channel. Volunteers holding a call to action were asked for a couple of minutes against three reflective prompts: where was I coming from when I volunteered, what has been leading me to think, decide and act as I have, and where should I go next. The first storyboard was 24 May 2024, on how we prepare ourselves and our families to handle emergencies. Theories included the Hawaiian concepts of ohana and calabash, where family extends past the household to friendships and chosen kin, alongside godparents and a designated support network, and relatives near or distant who can come in during a time of need. Applications came from military practice: the family care plan and the bug out bag. The circle had noted divergent expectations in the United States over whether adult children are looked to as carers for aging parents at all, or whether each generation is held responsible for its own life. Sources and input: each state or province interprets which laws apply to a family emergency, with Medicaid and the contrast between Virginia and Texas as the example, so local law can diverge from federal law. Opportunities: end-of-life conversations are difficult and get deferred, and deferring them loads stress and financial burden onto the surviving family. Challenges: legal advice is expensive, and advance care options differ by jurisdiction.
beats.pullQuote: we recognize that no hands raise is is a choice.

beats.title: Filial responsibility, and the question nobody could answer
beats.summary: The report-back came from the participant who had offered to help the absent volunteer holding this inquiry. Contact had been brief, but one finding was brought back: Virginia has filial responsibility laws under which an adult child who has the ability to earn income is legally obliged to support a parent in need, and failure to support carries a fine of up to 500 dollars and up to twelve months in jail. Not every state has such a law, and each is a separate jurisdiction on the question. The finding had been met with disbelief until it was checked. The facilitator undertook to bring the refined storyboard back to the absent volunteer as encouragement to keep going, and named plainly that life gets in the way and that these gatherings keep each other accountable. The questions-only round then opened. What happens when a death occurs in one state and the surviving family lives in another, and can one state enforce in another jurisdiction. What happens when the family lives in another country altogether, and whether one state's obligation can reach across an international border at all. One participant reasoned that residence in a state ought to bind regardless of where a person is at that moment, but said that international borders defeated them entirely. Another noted a comparable obligation in China, said outright that they disagreed with the Virginia law and could give philosophical reasons, and asked instead how it came about, who started it, and what the discussion was at the time. Nobody in the room knew the genesis. The participant who had researched the statute offered to do that forensic work with the absent volunteer before the next Lyceum. The facilitator's own note was that placing legal or financial responsibility on someone who may be unable to assume it is questionable, and that the storyboard would be refined for families burdened by the prospect of invoking an advance care option or a family care plan.

beats.title: A modern work ethic, and a team of three
beats.summary: The 30 June 2024 storyboard asked what we should strive for in a modern work ethic. Theories drew a parallel between a military and a civilian workplace: an anecdote of female naval engineers as the all-stars while men in the same workspace needed a guiding hand, set against a medical field where women students were perceived as ready to go and men less so. The contrast led the circle to ask why women appear to work twice as hard for the same success. Applications: hiring panels asking questions that actually test soft skills rather than pedigree, including how much struggle a candidate has come through, and reference checks aimed at whether someone is a team player, keeps a positive attitude and keeps learning, rather than at duties performed. Sources and input: intercultural skill and the ability to code switch in globalized teams working over video, and a willingness to learn another person's background instead of leaning only on one's own. Regulations were thin, beyond a need to distinguish private from public sector. Opportunities: investing in human capital through paid time off and retirement contributions, and interviewing employees to inform engagement rather than dictating from policy written long ago. Challenges: loyalty to a single company is gone, and organizations must adapt or watch people leave. Two calls to action had been recorded: a book, Athena Rising, on how men can act as role models to open opportunity and culture for women who may feel they have no voice, and an offer to report back from conversations with a small engineering team the volunteer supervises. That report-back followed. The environment they described was not toxic but unsupportive: nobody obstructed them and nobody mentored them, and their professional growth suffered for it. What worked was doing for them what one would do for any young engineer, paying attention, asking questions that are not yes or no, and taking a sincere interest in their development. A story from earlier service carried the point. On the pier, a slight male sailor struggling to lift a box would be helped by everyone; a woman of the same build would be walked past, on the reasoning that she had joined the navy and could figure it out.
beats.pullQuote: nobody was going out of their way to purposely trip them up, but nobody was actively engaged in providing mentorship to them.
beats.slideHint: The June 2024 storyboard six-panel with the work ethic question at the top, soft skills and code switching called out in the applications and sources panels, and the call to action bar naming the book Athena Rising and an update from a a small engineering team. A pull panel beside it holds the pier anecdote as two silhouettes with a box, one helped and one passed by.

beats.title: Questions only: AI, and policies written before the tools
beats.summary: After a pause for the circle to collect itself, the round produced the evening's most forward-leaning question: what artificial intelligence does to a modern work ethic, what it threatens, what it might replace, and where human soft skills stay ahead. The same participant remarked that the meeting already had an unacknowledged member present. The facilitator added a second question, whether a modern work ethic requires an overhaul of company and organizational policies written before the rapid increase of technology, taking the corporations that started the trend toward social media as the test case and treating any policy left unrevised as an opportunity to re-engage for everyone's well-being. The answer that came was honest about its own limits: no view on AI, but telework had been the long struggle in government service. The technology exists, the call itself proves it, and adoption is still slow behind we have always done it this way and it will never work, while smaller companies and organizations have embraced it and found it effective.
beats.pullQuote: I think we we have an unacknowledged member here as well, joining this meeting.

A footnote records that the round noted an unacknowledged member in the meeting.

beats.title: Housing, and a first year in a new city
beats.summary: The 4 August 2024 storyboard asked how we can help families afford housing in our community. Theories came from the housing market: local farmers underbidding on homes sold at auction so that a family facing eviction could be supported, the scale of the profit incentive in real estate, and tourist destinations where landlords earn more from short-term rentals than from permanent residents who might build wealth through ownership. Applications: Finland, with federal mandates for low rent and rent control capping what rent can reach so that working families have somewhere to live; New York City, where one generation benefited from affordable housing and the benefit was not passed to the next, leaving rapid rent increases falling on people unsure they can pay; and Hampton Roads, where private companies profit from the scale of military bureaucracy by running off-post housing of questionable quality. Sources and input: the color of law, and the systemic racism running through housing policy. Regulations: the Fair Housing Act of 1968 was passed, but implemented in a way that has left people and families of color out of ownership and stuck in a cycle of renting. Homelessness was named as a multi-spectrum issue, converging affordable housing, lack of employment and lack of credit, and so complex that the complexity itself paralyzes people out of taking part. Further policy options were rent to own, limiting private development in favor of public development, and community land trusts that let nonprofits hold space while tenants purchase the housing on it. Opportunities: the Broad Creek complex in Norfolk, Virginia as a possible rent-to-own model, and extending housing benefits to workers in critical fields so they can plant roots in a community rather than commute from a distant suburb. Challenges: housing is an interagency effort that is routinely read as one agency's sole responsibility. The report-back came from the participant who took this call to action. The first year had gone on understanding the environment and who is in it, followed by meetings with several nonprofits in the Downtown Eastside who approach unhoused people from different angles. The cycle they described has no entry point: employment requires an address, and someone unhoused has no address. There was hope on offer too, in organizations holding nonprofit housing and government officials accountable for taking public money and paying staff while single room occupancy homes stay as they are. Without rent control and a concerted effort between government and private enterprise, a growing city pushes more people into being unhoused.
beats.pullQuote: you can't apply for employment unless you have an address, but because they're unhoused, they don't have an address
beats.slideHint: The August 2024 storyboard six-panel with the housing question at the top, and the international examples named in the applications panel: Finland rent caps, New York City across generations, Hampton Roads off-post housing. Beside it a small cycle diagram, no address to no job to no housing to no address, and an update strip for the Downtown Eastside nonprofits and the accountability organizations.

beats.title: A question left standing, then mentoring adolescents
beats.summary: The housing round produced one question: what incentive, if any, a city like Vancouver offers a private owner of a multifamily building to open a share of units to people in the situation just described. No answer came. After a long silence the response was that the topic is difficult, that the storyboard would keep being updated, and that this is not only Vancouver but any large population center where public and private sectors fail to act together. The questioner then asked whether they had been heard at all, having spoken at length unsure the mute button was off. They had been. The format absorbed the question rather than resolving it, which is what the format is for. The next storyboard was 15 September 2024, on how we mentor adolescents into adulthood. Theories: balance in parenting, guiding children with freedom that is not absolute; constant cultivation, moving a child through a checklist of life skills such as swimming, martial arts and the Scouts as the measure of preparation; and technology as a surrogate educator, supplying information that is sometimes validated and sometimes not. Applications: responsibility thrust on children early, by design or through unfortunate circumstance; living abroad in Germany increasing the opportunity for autonomy; Japan, where young children walking to and from school alone is a strict cultural norm from early elementary age; and in the United States a gap in access to caregivers created by design, where training and deployments leave a family with an absent caregiver and a condition for poverty. Sources and input: negotiation as a life skill, and the question of when children get to negotiate with caregivers for more autonomy, which arrives at different stages in different families; and access to quality mentors, including whether surrogate mentors arrive from extended family or local community when a caregiver is absent, and whether that absence seeds harmful coping mechanisms carried into adulthood. Policies: flexible work options and paid time off for employees with children as a route to parental involvement at school and in community events, rather than family time confined to weekends and holidays. Opportunities and challenges: what volunteer mentorship exists around schools and communities; which social media platforms are of higher quality, and when to start guiding children toward a safe presence online; learning what today's youth actually like so they can be met on their own terms rather than taught what their elders were taught; and a shortage of mentors in every community.
beats.pullQuote: allows us to guide children by giving freedom, but not absolute freedom.
beats.slideHint: Split slide. Left, a single unanswered question in a box: what incentives does a city give a private multifamily owner to open units, carried forward. Right, the September 2024 storyboard six-panel with the mentoring question at the top, constant cultivation and technology as surrogate educator named in theories, and Germany and Japan set against the United States caregiver gap in applications.

beats.title: What mentorship actually looks like
beats.summary: This inquiry's call to action had been taken by two participants, one of them absent. The absent one had planned to use social media and research to see how different communities address mentorship, from the local level up to the international. The other had offered to find organizations that encourage mentorship and good examples worth copying, and gave the report. A general internet search turns up a plethora of organizations, most of them aimed at at-risk youth and most concentrated on high school age. Named were the YMCA, behavioral health services in various states, the Up Center, the Boys and Girls Club of America, and Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts as a form of mentorship in themselves. The pattern is consistent: a mentor signs up, picks a mentee, and commits a couple of hours a week, under a state, federal or city programme, inside a school system, or through a nonprofit. The clearest example found was the Up Center's Team Up, running since 2008 for ages 6 to 17. Mentorship also tends to be rooted in whatever activity is already in a person's life: the volunteer became a certified official with USA Swimming and now gives monthly hours to officiating meets. One avenue named but not yet pursued was a school-based youth programme. Beyond programmes, the report was about ordinary conversation, asking young people why they do what they do, why they attend to social media, what they are studying, and what they intend after high school, whether college or a vocational programme, without taking the shape of a parent. Recent graduates named a car as the first goal and had not considered putting money aside toward a house or any longer-term aim. Reading was part of the work, including the book already recorded against the work ethic inquiry. A chat contribution was read out mid-report and correctly reassigned: a Los Angeles nonprofit that empowers its community on housing rights, which belongs to the August inquiry rather than this one. The report closed with an offer to take any question from the group into further research and return with more.
beats.pullQuote: all kinds of opportunities that can stem from just simple conversations with these youths
beats.slideHint: A landscape slide of mentorship organizations as logos or plain name tiles: YMCA, state behavioral health services, the Up Center and Team Up with its 2008 start and 6 to 17 age band, Boys and Girls Club of America, Boy Scouts, Girl Scouts, USA Swimming. A sidebar headed What it takes lists a couple of hours a week, pick a mentee, start from an activity you are already in, and simple conversations about goals.

beats.title: The gap after seventeen
beats.summary: The facilitator opened the round with a question about the edge of the age band. Legal adulthood in the United States arrives at 18, and the years from 18 to 28 are a vulnerable stretch in which a young adult is answerable in law for their own decisions. The mentorship organizations named ran to 17. So do organizations continue past that line, and do any of them pass the torch across it, into the years where decisions carry legal consequences under each country's definitions. One participant, on a difficult connection, said they would have to research what exists for that age band, and confirmed the inquiry's own range as fifteen and up into adulthood. Another pushed in the opposite direction: a terrible decision at 16 can be permanent in some jurisdictions, so the plug was for earlier interdiction. It is hard to mentor a child out of a life-altering decision after the fact, and harder still from behind bars, when mentorship beforehand might have made the difference. The response accepted the point, that earlier is proactive rather than reactive, and turned it into the round's second question: how do organizations determine who counts as at-risk youth. Is it behavior already committed, or having been caught, or some other factor that marks a group as at risk before anything has gone wrong, and what criteria decide who gets mentorship and who does not.
beats.pullQuote: I hate to mentor a child after he or she has already made a life altering decision.
beats.slideHint: A timeline bar from age 6 to 28 with the mentorship programmes shaded 6 to 17, legal adulthood marked at 18, and the 18 to 28 stretch left blank and labelled as the gap. Two collected questions run underneath: who passes the torch across 18, and what criteria define at-risk before anything has happened.

beats.title: Before they leave high school
beats.summary: One participant, through a poor connection and audibly working to get the thought out, made the case for mentoring before a young person leaves high school, with a counsellor or professional based inside the school. In certain communities that person is hard to come by or not provided at all. The point was not careers advice but availability: someone there to talk to, and someone who can help a young person search for the feeling within that indicates what they might want to do. The facilitator agreed and complicated it. Student support services in Canada are one model of exactly that, but a school without those staff, or with a single guidance counsellor for an entire student body, cannot deliver it, and the result is a lack of resources to ensure students are informed or guided. Influences also depend on place: military recruiters came into the high school of a military town to pitch service after graduation, and towns without that presence have to work out for themselves which outside agencies or entities come in and hold those conversations. The note was taken for the storyboard, tied back to the earlier point that mentoring someone after a decision is already on their record is uphill work that active mentorship might have made unnecessary.
beats.pullQuote: If there's only one guidance counselor for an entire student body
beats.slideHint: A school-shaped panel listing what a young person can reach inside the building: a counsellor or support service, a teacher, an outside agency that visits. Beside it a scarcity note, one guidance counsellor for an entire student body, and a second panel contrasting a military town where recruiters visit with a town where nobody comes in at all.

beats.title: Coexistence with nature, and a note on the artifact itself
beats.summary: The last storyboard was 20 October 2024, on how we cultivate peaceful coexistence with nature in our communities. Theories and examples were international. The Ganges is a holy site to its population and is flooded with toxic waste brought by industry and by the results of religious ceremony. Venus was once like Earth until climate change altered its atmosphere and made it uninhabitable, read as a possible warning of what Earth could become without action. Applications: India using its court system to extend rights to land, water and air in the way human rights are understood; and in Virginia, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation taking a grassroots approach to building a culture of caring about a watershed regardless of a person's industry or private life. Sources and input: an uncomfortable truth, that a psychological barrier against discomfort leads people to disengage from a complex and real problem, choosing not to confront what is happening to them and limiting their own citizenship in the process; and the need for those holding the levers of power, corporations and governments, to lead by example so that communities can act. Regulations and policies: what the world looked like during and after Covid, with photographs of Los Angeles under blue sky and less smog than on a typical day before; and environmental racism, where marginalized populations face greater health hazards from unhealthy environments, unclean drinking water and land too contaminated to farm. Opportunities: increasing indigenous governance so that indigenous knowledge and wisdom shape current policy, with the David Suzuki Foundation in Canada as the example; and bringing children into nature conservation through routine play and exploration inside the regular school curriculum. Challenges: cultural wisdom requires engaging an older population about what worked for them and how to pass it on; and collectivist ideas do not resonate where thinking leans purely capitalist, which makes shaping minds toward the collective a challenge in itself. This inquiry's call to action had not moved. The planned conversation with a local beekeeper about organizing the protection of pollinators did not happen because both parties were on leave, and it was carried over, with an invitation for the beekeeper to speak briefly at a future Lyceum. The facilitator named this as the accountability part of the practice, holding each other to what was said. The co-facilitator then made an administrative point about the storyboard on screen: unlike the earlier boards, its entries are hyperlinked in blue to the sources behind them, the summaries are being hung on the website and in a few other places, copies can be sent by email on request, and the group was asked directly for ideas to improve the format. The facilitator's closing questions for the round were whether organizations inside government encourage sustainable practices and whether those examples are highlighted in a way that draws people in, and the same question of the private sector, where wealth and resources spent on sustainability may be going unreported in an atmosphere of fear that prevents shared understanding on climate change.
beats.pullQuote: People choose not to confront this as it's happening to them. So therefore, they just choose not to engage, and therefore they're limiting their citizenship in their community.
beats.slideHint: The October 2024 storyboard six-panel with the nature question at the top and its entries visibly hyperlinked in blue, the difference from earlier boards called out in a small margin note. The Ganges, Venus, India's courts, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation and the David Suzuki Foundation appear as named tiles, with the Los Angeles before and during Covid photographs paired in the policies panel. The call to action bar is marked carried forward.

beats.title: Administrative notes, and the fellowship circle
beats.summary: The website was pointed to as the place where examples of cross-cultural learning are written up so that a reader can apply them in their own community, with links there to the group's Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and Quora presence. A survey tool is in development for use in later gatherings, and until then feedback goes through the message form on the site's homepage or directly to either facilitator, on the sequence of inquiry or on this evening's sequence for reflection. Before closing, the facilitator acknowledged a reading shared in the chat on how AI may be affecting work now and in future, an essay by the chief executive of Anthropic together with a long recorded interview with the same author, confirmed that it answered the earlier question raised in the work ethic round, and assigned it to that storyboard. The fellowship circle then opened. One participant offered a visit to the Grand Canyon that week: its permanence and its age put much of what the circle discusses into proportion, and what was offered was not an answer but an open-ended thought about feeling insignificant standing beside it. Another, returning after missing the previous forum, tied the vision and purpose in the group's statement to balancing enduring truths and what is really important in life against the tyranny of a hectic present, in a period of hectic current events, and said it was good to be in the circle. Another was glad to have made this gathering after missing several, having now heard the important topics that had been missed, and hoped that as the group moves forward it will reach conclusions that help each other and the wider community. Another said they wished they could go back in time and attend the ones they had skipped. The facilitator closed by naming where the circle had joined from that night, Canada, Los Angeles, Pittsburgh and Virginia, as an interconnection between different communities already in existence and a small example of what a larger version would look like, and read the motto: our lives are our own and each person walks their own path, but the journey is collective, for humanity and the natural world.
beats.pullQuote: We're all walking our path of life. But it's our collective journey.
beats.slideHint: An administrative slide with the website address, the four social media names, and a line reading survey tool in development with a feedback route. Then a closing slide holding the motto, this is your life and our journey for humanity and the natural world, over a plain map with four unlabelled markers for Canada, Los Angeles, Pittsburgh and Virginia.

beats.title: After the close: how a newcomer gets in
beats.summary: The recording continued past the formal close, with the facilitators and a newer participant staying on to work through onboarding. The problem was stated plainly. The group's video calls and collaborative work normally run on Microsoft Teams; the core few operate there at an administrative level, and new people are fitted into different levels of trust and different slots as they arrive. An onboarding team and a channel of instructions already exist, but reading them requires already being on Teams and knowing how to navigate it, which anyone outside the military or a large corporate employer that pays for the platform may not. Some in the circle are still getting used to it. What is needed is a comprehensive checklist, by the book, that can be sent to a person before they have an account, and modelled on what an incoming member actually encounters. This is the only forward-looking commitment of the evening that belongs to no inquiry.
beats.slideHint: A simple onboarding funnel: invitation by email, account created, platform basics, onboarding channel, tiers of access. Each step carries the blocker beside it, with the platform-literacy assumption marked as the point where newcomers stall, and a note that the checklist to be written must work before any account exists.
